prompt: A walker and a jogger travel along the same straight line in the same direction. The walker walks at one meter per second, while the jogger runs at two meters per second. The jogger starts one meter in front of the walker. A dog starts with the walker, and then runs back and forth between the walker and the jogger with constant speed of three meters per second. Let $f(n)$ meters denote the total distance travelled by the dog when it has returned to the walker for the $n$th time (so $f(0)=0$). Find a formula for $f(n)$.

solutions.title: One round trip multiplies the gap by 5/2
solutions.body:
Let $x_n$ be the distance between the walker and the jogger at the moment the dog returns to the walker for the $n$th time; $x_0=1$. All distances are in meters, times in seconds.

**One round trip.** Suppose the gap is $x$ and the dog is at the walker.
- *Going out.* The dog (speed 3) chases the jogger (speed 2), closing at $3-2=1$ m/s, so it reaches the jogger after $x$ seconds. Meanwhile the gap between walker and jogger grows at $2-1=1$ m/s, so it is now $2x$.
- *Coming back.* Dog and walker approach each other at $3+1=4$ m/s, so this takes $\frac{2x}{4}=\frac x2$ seconds, during which the gap grows by another $\frac x2$.

So one round trip takes $x+\frac x2=\frac{3x}{2}$ seconds, the dog runs $3\cdot\frac{3x}{2}=\frac{9x}{2}$ meters, and the new gap is $2x+\frac x2=\frac{5x}{2}$.

**Summing.** Hence $x_k=\left(\frac52\right)^k$ and the $k$th trip (starting with gap $x_{k-1}$) has length $\frac92\left(\frac52\right)^{k-1}$. Therefore
$$f(n)=\frac92\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\frac52\right)^{k-1}=\frac92\cdot\frac{(5/2)^n-1}{5/2-1}=3\left(\left(\frac52\right)^n-1\right).$$

*Check:* $n=1$: the dog runs $3$ m out (1 s) and $1.5$ m back (0.5 s), total $4.5=3\left(\frac52-1\right)$.

**Answer:** $f(n)=3\left(\left(\frac52\right)^n-1\right)$.

solutions.title: Total time instead of total distance
solutions.body:
Since the dog always runs at 3 m/s, $f(n)=3T_n$ where $T_n$ is the time of the $n$th return. The gap between walker and jogger at time $t$ is $1+t$ (it grows at 1 m/s).

Work in the walker's frame: there the jogger moves away at 1 m/s, and the dog moves at $2$ m/s outwards and $4$ m/s inwards. If the dog leaves the walker at time $t$ (gap $1+t$), it catches the jogger at the time $s$ with $2(s-t)=(1+t)+(s-t)$, i.e. $s=2t+1$. Coming back it covers the gap $1+s$ at 4 m/s, taking $\frac{1+s}{4}$. So the next return time is
$$t'=s+\frac{1+s}{4}=\frac{5s+1}{4},\quad s=2t+1\ \Rightarrow\ t'=\frac{10t+6}{4}=\frac{5t+3}{2}.$$
Thus $T_n+1=\frac52(T_{n-1}+1)$ with $T_0=0$, so $T_n=\left(\frac52\right)^n-1$ and $f(n)=3T_n=3\left(\left(\frac52\right)^n-1\right)$.

solutions.title: Count factors of 10, then use divisibility by 999999
solutions.body:
**The last nine digits.** The multiples of $5$ up to $40$ are $5,10,15,20,25,30,35,40$; they contribute one factor $5$ each, and $25$ contributes one more, so $5^9\,\|\,40!$. There are far more than nine factors of $2$ (already $\lfloor 40/2\rfloor=20$ even numbers). Hence $10^9\mid 40!$, so the last nine digits are zero:
$$p=q=r=s=t=u=v=w=x=0.$$

**The first six digits.** We have $999999=10^6-1=27\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot37$, and these factors $27,7,11,13,37$ are pairwise coprime and each at most $40$ (with $27=3^3$ and $3^{18}\mid40!$), so $999999\mid 40!$.

Since $10^6\equiv1\pmod{999999}$, a number is congruent mod $999999$ to the sum of its six-digit blocks taken from the right. The blocks of $40!$ are
$$abcdef,\ 283247,\ 897734,\ 345611,\ 269596,\ 115894,\ 272pqr=272000,\ stuvwx=000000.$$
Their sum is $abcdef+2184082$, which must be a multiple of $999999$. As $0\le abcdef\le 999999$, we get $2184082<abcdef+2184082<3184082$, so the multiple is $3\cdot999999=2999997$ and
$$abcdef=2999997-2184082=815915.$$

*Check:* the digit sum is $(8+1+5+9+1+5)+160=29+160=189=21\cdot9$, consistent with $9\mid40!$. Indeed $40!=815915283247897734345611269596115894272000000000$.

**Answer:** $p=q=\dots=x=0$ and $a,b,c,d,e,f=8,1,5,9,1,5$ (so $abcdef=815915$).

solutions.title: Differentiate, substitute, differentiate again
solutions.body:
**First derivative.** Write $f(x)=\int_0^x G(x,v)\,dv$ with $G(x,v)=\int_0^x e^{u^2v^2}\,du$. By the Leibniz rule,
$$f'(x)=G(x,x)+\int_0^x\frac{\partial G}{\partial x}(x,v)\,dv=\int_0^x e^{u^2x^2}\,du+\int_0^x e^{x^2v^2}\,dv=2\int_0^x e^{x^2v^2}\,dv .$$
(Equivalently: the integrand is symmetric in $u,v$, so $f(x)=2\int_0^x\!\int_0^u e^{u^2v^2}\,dv\,du$, and then the fundamental theorem of calculus gives the same formula.)

**Substitution.** For $x>0$ put $t=xv$, $dv=dt/x$:
$$f'(x)=\frac2x\int_0^{x^2}e^{t^2}\,dt .$$

**Second derivative.** By the product rule and the fundamental theorem of calculus,
$$f''(x)=-\frac{2}{x^2}\int_0^{x^2}e^{t^2}\,dt+\frac2x\cdot e^{x^4}\cdot 2x=-\frac{2}{x^2}\int_0^{x^2}e^{t^2}\,dt+4e^{x^4}.$$

**Combine.** The integral cancels in
$$x f''(x)+f'(x)=-\frac2x\int_0^{x^2}e^{t^2}dt+4xe^{x^4}+\frac2x\int_0^{x^2}e^{t^2}dt=4xe^{x^4}.$$
At $x=2$: $2f''(2)+f'(2)=8e^{16}\approx 7.11\times10^{7}$.

**Answer:** $8e^{16}$.

solutions.title: Recognise a derivative of a product
solutions.body:
Note $xf''(x)+f'(x)=\big(xf'(x)\big)'$. From $f'(x)=\frac2x\int_0^{x^2}e^{t^2}dt$ (derived as in the first solution) we get
$$xf'(x)=2\int_0^{x^2}e^{t^2}\,dt,\qquad \big(xf'(x)\big)'=2e^{x^4}\cdot 2x=4xe^{x^4}.$$
So $2f''(2)+f'(2)=\big(xf'\big)'(2)=8e^{16}$. (A numerical check of the double integral confirms $\approx 71\,088\,884.16$.)

prompt: Two circles $\alpha,\beta$ touch externally at the point $X$. Let $A,P$ be two distinct points on $\alpha$ different from $X$, and let $AX$ and $PX$ meet $\beta$ again in the points $B$ and $Q$ respectively. Prove that $AP$ is parallel to $QB$.
answer: The homothety with centre $X$ (negative ratio) taking $\alpha$ to $\beta$ maps $A\mapsto B$, $P\mapsto Q$; equivalently, angle chase with the common tangent at $X$.

solutions.title: Common tangent and the tangent–chord angle
solutions.body:
Let $t$ be the common tangent to $\alpha$ and $\beta$ at $X$. To avoid case distinctions we use directed angles between lines, taken mod $180^\circ$: $\measuredangle(\ell,m)$ is the angle through which line $\ell$ must be rotated (counterclockwise) to become parallel to $m$. In this language the tangent–chord theorem says: if $U,V$ are on a circle with tangent $t$ at $X$, then $\measuredangle(VX,VU)=\measuredangle(t,XU)$ (the limiting case $V\to X$ of the inscribed angle theorem).

- Tangent–chord in $\alpha$ ($U=A$, $V=P$): $\measuredangle(PX,PA)=\measuredangle(t,XA)$.
- Tangent–chord in $\beta$ ($U=B$, $V=Q$): $\measuredangle(QX,QB)=\measuredangle(t,XB)$.

But $XA$ and $XB$ are the same line $AB$, and $PX$ and $QX$ are the same line $\ell$. Hence
$$\measuredangle(\ell,PA)=\measuredangle(t,AB)=\measuredangle(\ell,QB).$$
Two lines making the same directed angle with the line $\ell$ are parallel, so $AP\parallel QB$. (They are distinct lines since $A\notin\beta$.) ∎

solutions.title: Homothety
solutions.body:
Let $O_1,O_2$ and $r_1,r_2$ be the centres and radii of $\alpha,\beta$. External tangency means $X$ lies on segment $O_1O_2$ with $XO_1=r_1$, $XO_2=r_2$. Let $h$ be the homothety with centre $X$ and ratio $-\frac{r_2}{r_1}$. Then $h(O_1)$ is the point on ray opposite to $XO_1$ at distance $r_2$, i.e. $O_2$, and $h$ multiplies distances by $\frac{r_2}{r_1}$; so $h(\alpha)$ is the circle with centre $O_2$ and radius $r_2$, which is $\beta$.

A homothety centred at $X$ maps every line through $X$ to itself. So $h(A)$ lies on $\beta$ and on line $AX$, and $h(A)\neq X$ because $A\ne X$ and $h$ is injective with $h(X)=X$. The line $AX$ meets $\beta$ only at $X$ and $B$, so $h(A)=B$. Likewise $h(P)=Q$.

A homothety maps every line to a parallel line, so the line $AP$ is mapped to the line $BQ$, which is parallel to $AP$. ∎

prompt: Let $\mathbb{C}$ denote the complex numbers and let $M_3(\mathbb{C})$ denote the $3$ by $3$ matrices with entries in $\mathbb{C}$. Suppose $A,B\in M_3(\mathbb{C})$, $B\neq0$, and $AB=0$ (where $0$ denotes the $3$ by $3$ matrix with all entries zero). Prove that there exists $0\neq D\in M_3(\mathbb{C})$ such that $AD=DA=0$.
answer: $A$ is singular, so its minimal polynomial is $m(X)=Xq(X)$ and $D=q(A)\neq0$ works (or $D=xy^{T}$ with $Ax=0$, $y^{T}A=0$).

solutions.title: Minimal polynomial
solutions.body:
**$A$ is singular.** If $A$ were invertible, then $B=A^{-1}(AB)=0$, contradicting $B\ne0$. So $0$ is an eigenvalue of $A$.

**Minimal polynomial.** Let $m(X)$ be the minimal polynomial of $A$: the monic polynomial of least degree with $m(A)=0$. Its roots are exactly the eigenvalues of $A$, so $m(0)=0$ and we can write $m(X)=X\,q(X)$ with $q$ a polynomial of degree $\deg m-1$ (if $\deg m=1$ then $q=1$).

Put $D=q(A)$. Since $\deg q<\deg m$ and $q\ne0$ is monic, minimality gives $D=q(A)\neq0$. And because powers of $A$ commute with $A$,
$$AD=Aq(A)=m(A)=0,\qquad DA=q(A)A=m(A)=0.$$
∎

solutions.title: A rank-one matrix built from kernels
solutions.body:
As above, $A$ is singular (else $B=A^{-1}AB=0$). So $\det A=\det A^{T}=0$, and there are nonzero column vectors $x,y\in\mathbb C^3$ with
$$Ax=0,\qquad A^{T}y=0\ \ (\text{i.e. } y^{T}A=0).$$
Let $D=xy^{T}$, a $3\times3$ matrix. Its $(i,j)$ entry is $x_iy_j$, and choosing $i,j$ with $x_i\ne0$, $y_j\ne0$ shows $D\ne0$. Finally
$$AD=(Ax)y^{T}=0,\qquad DA=x(y^{T}A)=0.$$
∎

prompt: Let $n$ be a nonzero integer. Prove that $n^4-7n^2+1$ can never be a perfect square (i.e. of the form $m^2$ for some integer $m$).
answer: $n^4-7n^2+1=(n^2-3n+1)(n^2+3n+1)$ with coprime factors, and $n^2+3n+1$ lies strictly between $(n+1)^2$ and $(n+2)^2$; or squeeze between $(n^2-4)^2$ and $(n^2-3)^2$.

solutions.title: Factor into coprime parts
solutions.body:
The expression depends only on $n^2$, so assume $n\ge1$. For $n=1,2$ the value is $-5,-11<0$, not a square. Let $n\ge3$ and suppose $n^4-7n^2+1=m^2$. We have
$$n^4-7n^2+1=(n^2+1)^2-9n^2=(n^2-3n+1)(n^2+3n+1),$$
and both factors are positive for $n\ge3$ (as $n^2-3n+1=n(n-3)+1\ge1$).

**The factors are coprime.** Let a prime $p$ divide both. Then $p$ divides their difference $6n$, so $p\in\{2,3\}$ or $p\mid n$.
- If $p\mid n$: $n^2+3n+1\equiv1\pmod p$, impossible.
- $p=2$: $n^2+3n+1=n(n+3)+1$ is odd, since $n(n+3)$ is even.
- $p=3$: $n^2+3n+1\equiv n^2+1\equiv 1$ or $2\pmod 3$.

So $\gcd=1$. Two coprime positive integers whose product is a perfect square are both perfect squares (compare prime exponents). In particular $n^2+3n+1$ is a square. But for $n\ge1$,
$$(n+1)^2=n^2+2n+1<n^2+3n+1<n^2+4n+4=(n+2)^2,$$
so it lies strictly between consecutive squares — a contradiction. ∎

*(The official solution additionally reduces mod 3 to $n=3m$; that step is not needed.)*

solutions.title: Squeeze between consecutive squares
solutions.body:
Again take $n\ge1$. Compare $N=n^4-7n^2+1$ with
$$(n^2-3)^2=n^4-6n^2+9,\qquad (n^2-4)^2=n^4-8n^2+16.$$
We have $(n^2-3)^2-N=n^2+8>0$ and $N-(n^2-4)^2=n^2-15>0$ for $n\ge4$. For $n\ge4$, $n^2-4\ge 12>0$, so $N$ lies strictly between the consecutive squares $(n^2-4)^2$ and $(n^2-3)^2$ and is not a square.

The remaining cases: $n=1,2,3$ give $N=-5,-11,19$, none a perfect square. ∎

prompt: Does there exist a twice differentiable function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ such that $f'(x)=f(x+1)-f(x)$ for all $x$ and $f''(0)\neq0$? Justify your answer. (Here $\mathbb{R}$ denotes the real numbers and $f'$ denotes the derivative of $f$.)

solutions.title: Complex exponential solutions
solutions.body:
**Yes.** Linear functions $ax+b$ solve the equation but have $f''=0$, so we look for $f(x)=e^{rx}$ with $r\in\mathbb C$. Then $f'(x)=re^{rx}$ and $f(x+1)-f(x)=e^{rx}(e^r-1)$, so we need
$$e^{r}=1+r .$$

**A non-real root.** Write $r=a+ib$. The equation is $e^a\cos b=1+a$, $e^a\sin b=b$. Look for $b\in(2\pi,3\pi)$, where $\sin b>0$. Then the second equation forces $e^a=\frac{b}{\sin b}$, i.e. $a=\ln\frac{b}{\sin b}$, and the first becomes $h(b)=0$ with
$$h(b)=b\cot b-1-\ln\frac{b}{\sin b}.$$
$h$ is continuous on $(2\pi,3\pi)$.
- As $b\to2\pi^+$: put $s=\sin b\to0^+$. Then $b\cot b\approx \frac{2\pi}{s}$ while $\ln\frac bs\approx\ln\frac{2\pi}{s}$; since $\frac{c}{s}-\ln\frac{c}{s}\to+\infty$, $h(b)\to+\infty$.
- As $b\to3\pi^-$: $\cot b\to-\infty$ so $b\cot b\to-\infty$, and $-\ln\frac{b}{\sin b}\to-\infty$; so $h(b)\to-\infty$.

By the intermediate value theorem there is $q\in(2\pi,3\pi)$ with $h(q)=0$. Put $p=\ln\frac{q}{\sin q}$; then $e^{p}\sin q=q$ and $e^p\cos q=q\cot q=1+p$, so $r=p+iq$ satisfies $e^r=1+r$. Numerically $p\approx2.0888$, $q\approx7.4615$. Note $p>0$ because $q>1\ge\sin q$.

**A real solution.** For real $x$, $e^{rx}=e^{px}(\cos qx+i\sin qx)$. The equation $g'(x)=g(x+1)-g(x)$ is linear with real coefficients, so the imaginary part
$$f(x)=e^{px}\sin(qx)$$
also satisfies it. It is infinitely differentiable, and
$$f'(x)=e^{px}(p\sin qx+q\cos qx),\quad f''(x)=e^{px}\big((p^2-q^2)\sin qx+2pq\cos qx\big),$$
so $f''(0)=2pq\neq0$ since $p,q>0$.

**Answer: Yes.**
